hazards.catch-a-fish: You reached to scoop a young fish. Young fish are small and easily hurt. Watch them in the model channel or through the viewer, and leave the marsh's fish in the water.
hazards.chase-the-birds: You ran towards the birds. Parent birds leave their nests when people rush close, and the eggs get cold. Move slowly, stay on the boardwalk and use the binoculars to see them up close.
hazards.leave-the-boardwalk: You stepped off the boardwalk. Marsh mud is soft and can hold a boot fast, and feet crush nests and young plants. The boardwalk is there so people can watch without harming the nursery.
hazards.marsh-is-just-mud: You said the marsh is just mud. The mud and channels are full of small life: tiny crabs, worms and young fish. That food and shelter is why fish and birds raise their young here.

interrupts.alert: A flock of birds lifts off the mud near the boardwalk.
interrupts.cue: Stop still, stay quiet and let the birds settle again.
interrupts.missNote: The class kept moving and talking, and the flock flew off to the far side of the marsh.
interrupts.why: Birds lift when something startles them. Standing still and quiet shows them there is no danger, so they land again and keep feeding. The crew pauses its work the same way when birds are close.
interrupts.wrongNote: That keeps the birds startled. Stop still and stay quiet. Choose the response that deals with it now.

interrupts.alert: The crew lead asks why they plant grass along the channel edges.
interrupts.cue: Say the grass gives young fish and birds places to hide.
interrupts.missNote: You could not say why the grass matters, and the crew lead had to explain before the class could go on.
interrupts.why: Knowing why the grass matters shows you understand the nursery. Every clump along a channel is another hiding place. That is why the crew plants the edges first when it restores a marsh.
interrupts.wrongNote: That does not explain the grass. Say what young animals use it for. Choose the response that deals with it now.

lateNotes.esn-checkin: The check-in comes at the very end of the walk.
lateNotes.esn-marsh-log: The marsh record is written once you have seen each place — nothing to record yet.

name: The Tidal Marsh Nursery

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Mark the three things that help young fish and birds grow up here.

decoyNotes.esn-bench: A good place to rest, but not part of the nursery.

itemNames.esn-mud: the mud full of tiny animals

itemNotes.esn-grass: Young birds and fish hide here.
itemNotes.esn-mud: Plenty of food for the young.

steps.prompt: Mark the three things that help young fish and birds grow up here.
steps.title: Find what makes the marsh a nursery
steps.why: A nursery is a safe place for young animals to grow. In a tidal marsh, shallow channels keep out big fish that hunt, tall grass gives hiding places, and the mud is full of tiny animals to eat. Food, shelter and calm water together make the marsh a place where young life can start.

steps.cue: Walk slowly and quietly onto the boardwalk with the crew lead.
steps.prompt: Walk slowly and quietly onto the boardwalk with the crew lead.
steps.title: Move quietly onto the boardwalk
steps.why: Birds nesting in the marsh notice noise and quick movement. Walking slowly and talking quietly lets you watch without making parent birds leave their nests. The restoration crew works the same way, calmly and gently, so the nursery stays a calm place.

steps.cue: Put the steps of the tide coming into the marsh and going out in order.

itemNames.esn-ord-birds: 4 · birds feed on the open mud
itemNames.esn-ord-fall: 3 · the tide falls and the channels drain
itemNames.esn-ord-fish: 2 · young fish swim in to feed and hide
itemNames.esn-ord-rise: 1 · the tide rises into the channels

steps.outOfOrderNote: Out of order. Start with the tide rising into the channels.
steps.prompt: Put the steps of the tide coming into the marsh and going out in order.
steps.title: Put the tide's visit in order
steps.why: Twice a day the tide rises and falls. As it rises, water fills the channels and brings in young fish and food. As it falls, the channels drain and the mud is left for birds to feed on. Knowing this order explains why the marsh is busy at every stage of the tide.

steps.cue: Hold the underwater viewer still until the young fish come back.
steps.holdBreakNote: The viewer moved and the fish darted off. Hold it still again and wait.
steps.prompt: Hold the underwater viewer still until the young fish come back.
steps.title: Hold the viewer still over the channel
steps.why: Young fish dart away from movement and come back when all is calm. Holding the viewer still for a while lets them return so you can see them. Patience is a big part of watching wildlife, and the crew counts fish in exactly this careful way.

steps.cue: Turn the focus wheel until the nest across the channel is sharp.
steps.prompt: Turn the focus wheel until the nest across the channel is sharp.
steps.title: Focus the binoculars
steps.why: Binoculars let you see small things from far away, so you do not need to go closer. A sharp picture helps you notice details, like how the nest is hidden in the grass. Good watching from a distance is how scientists study animals without disturbing them.

steps.cue: Commit when the marker sits at the water line on the channel post.

gauge.label: TIDE
gauge.missNote: Not at the water line. Read where the water meets the post.

steps.prompt: Commit when the marker sits at the water line on the channel post.
steps.title: Read the water level in the model channel
steps.why: The model channel shows the tide rising and falling. Reading the water line on the post shows how deep the channel is right now. Shallow water is the key to the nursery, because it keeps the big hunters out while the small fish stay safe.

steps.cue: Drag the model grass clump to the bare edge of the channel.

drag.missNote: Not on the bare edge yet. Place it where the channel has no grass.

steps.prompt: Drag the model grass clump to the bare edge of the channel.
steps.title: Place the grass clump in the model marsh
steps.why: The restoration crew plants grass along bare channel edges so young fish have more hiding places. Putting the model clump on the bare edge shows how each new plant adds shelter. A marsh with more grass along its channels can shelter more young animals.

steps.cue: Choose the sentence that says why young animals start life here.
steps.prompt: Choose the sentence that says why young animals start life here.
steps.title: Say why the marsh is a nursery
steps.why: You saw food in the mud, hiding places in the grass and shallow water that keeps big hunters away. A good answer puts those together: the marsh is a nursery because it gives young animals food and shelter. It says what you saw and nothing more.

steps.cue: Look from the boardwalk and mark each young animal you can see.

decoyNotes.esn-gull: A lovely bird, but a grown-up, not a young one.

itemNames.esn-nest: a nest tucked in the grass

itemNotes.esn-fry: Young fish growing in calm water.

steps.prompt: Look from the boardwalk and mark each young animal you can see.
steps.title: Spot the young animals in the marsh
steps.why: Spotting young animals is proof that the nursery is working. A line of ducklings behind a parent, tiny fish in a channel and a nest tucked in the grass all show that the marsh is doing its job. Crews use sightings like these to know a restored marsh is healthy.

steps.cue: Keep the marker on one young fish as it swims into the grass.
steps.holdBreakNote: The marker lost the fish. Find it again and follow it into the grass.
steps.prompt: Keep the marker on one young fish as it swims into the grass.
steps.title: Follow a young fish along the channel
steps.why: Following one fish shows how it uses the marsh. It swims along the shallow channel, then slips into the grass when something moves. Watching that shows you exactly why the grass edges matter so much to the nursery.

steps.cue: Write one line for the channel, the grass and the mud.
steps.prompt: Write one line for the channel, the grass and the mud.
steps.title: Record what you saw at each place
steps.why: A short note for each place shows how the parts of the marsh work together. Anyone reading your notes can see where the young animals were and why. The crew keeps records the same way, so they can compare the marsh from year to year.

steps.cue: Put your notes next to another group's and look for the same animals.
steps.prompt: Put your notes next to another group's and look for the same animals.
steps.title: Compare sightings with another group
steps.why: Two groups watching the same marsh may see different things. Comparing notes gives a fuller picture of the nursery. Scientists share sightings in the same way, because many careful watchers see more than one.

steps.cue: Why is the marsh a nursery? What is one way people keep it calm?
steps.prompt: Why is the marsh a nursery? What is one way people keep it calm?
steps.title: Check in before leaving the boardwalk
steps.why: The crew talks about the day before leaving, and the class does the same. Each learner says one reason the marsh is a nursery and one way visitors help. If anyone thinks the marsh is just empty mud, the group sorts it out now.
